results.text:
Ranked: Top 10 portable power stations for watt-hours per dollar (2026) 
 Skip to main content 
 Metric Shootouts 
 Portable Power Stations for Watt-Hours per Dollar: The 2026 Ranked List
 Paravolta Architecture Desk Updated October 2026 7 min read 
 Ten portable power stations ranked by watt-hours per dollar at today's store price and at full price, plus how bare batteries and small units compare.
 At today’s store price, the Pecron E3600LFP stores the most energy per dollar of any all-in-one portable power station we list, about 3.08 Wh per dollar, but only while its sale lasts. The BLUETTI Elite 400 comes next at 2.74 at its regular price, then the Renogy PowerStation 2000 at 2.41. Bare LiFePO4 batteries such as the EG4 WallMount All Weather 280Ah score higher, about 4.59, but they need a separate inverter, and small units like the EcoFlow RIVER 3 Plus cost the most per watt-hour, at about 0.96.
 Ranked: Top 10 Portable Power Stations for Watt-Hours per Dollar (2026)
 We divided each unit’s rated capacity by its price. Prices were checked on October 27, 2026, and they change often, so treat the order as a snapshot.
 We ran the number two ways: at today’s store price, and at the full price the store shows crossed out. Sales come and go, so the full-price column shows which units hold up when the sale ends.
 Rank Model Capacity Today’s price Wh per $ today Wh per $ at full price

 2 BLUETTI Elite 400 3,840 Wh $1,399 2.74 2.74 
 3 Renogy PowerStation 2000 2,048 Wh $849 2.41 2.41 
 4 BLUETTI Elite 100 mini 1,004.8 Wh $429 2.34 2.34 
 5 ALLPOWERS P1800 1,024 Wh $439 (full $1,059.98) 2.33 0.97 
 6 BLUETTI AC180 1,152 Wh $499 2.31 2.31 
 7 BLUETTI Elite 200 V2 2,073.6 Wh $899 2.31 2.31 
 8 EcoFlow DELTA 3 Max 2,048 Wh $899 (full $1,199) 2.28 1.71 
 9 Jackery HomePower 3000 3,072 Wh $1,349 (full $1,499) 2.28 2.05 
 10 EcoFlow DELTA 3 Ultra 3,072 Wh $1,349 (full $1,599) 2.28 1.92 
 All-in-one portable power stations, ranked by watt-hours per dollar at today’s store price, with the full-price figure breaking a tie, checked October 27, 2026. How We Ranked Them
 Every unit was scored the same way, like comparing the cost per gallon at two gas stations. We use today’s price, not an average, because that is what you would pay if you bought it now.
 Step 1: take the capacity in Wh from the maker’s spec sheet.
 Step 2: take today’s price from the store page.
 Step 3: divide the first by the second.
 Example: the Renogy PowerStation 2000 holds 2,048 Wh for $849, which is about 2.41 Wh per dollar.
 We only list units sold in the US that you can buy through Paravolta today. A unit that is sold out, retired or no longer made is left off, even if its old price looked good.
 This only measures storage per dollar. It says nothing about output, cycle life or charging speed, which is why the sections below add those back in.
 The Top 3 Value Leaders
 The Pecron E3600LFP tops the list at 3,072 Wh for $999, about 33 cents per watt-hour, but that is a sale price. At its full price of $1,999 it drops to about 1.54 Wh per dollar, which would put it well down this list.
 The BLUETTI Elite 400 comes second at 3,840 Wh for $1,399, about 36 cents per watt-hour, and that is its regular price, so it leads once sales end. The Renogy PowerStation 2000 is third at 2,048 Wh for $849, also its regular price.
 Mid-Pack Units Still Worth a Look
 The BLUETTI Elite 100 mini (2.34) and the ALLPOWERS P1800 (2.33) come next, but the P1800’s figure is a sale price: at its full price of $1,059.98 it falls to about 0.97. The BLUETTI AC180 and the BLUETTI Elite 200 V2 both land at about 2.31, even though one is nearly twice the size of the other. The AC180 holds 1,152 Wh for $499; the Elite 200 V2 holds 2,073.6 Wh for $899.
 The EcoFlow DELTA 3 Max, the Jackery HomePower 3000 and the EcoFlow DELTA 3 Ultra sit right behind at about 2.28, all on sale prices, with the Jackery Explorer 2000 v2 just outside the top 10 at 2.27.
 Bare LiFePO4 Batteries Score Higher, but Need More Parts
 Six batteries beat every power station above on this measure. They are not power stations at all, so they are not ranked in the table.
 Battery Capacity Today’s price Wh per dollar 
 EG4 WallMount All Weather 280Ah (battery only) 14,336 Wh $3,124.99 4.59 
 Renogy Core Mini 12V 300Ah (battery only) 3,840 Wh $879.99 4.36 
 EG4 WallMount Indoor 314Ah (battery only) 16,000 Wh $3,739 4.28 
 Rich Solar ALPHA 5 PRO 48V 100Ah (battery only) 5,120 Wh $1,249 4.10

 Bare batteries, today’s store price, checked October 27, 2026. Three of them are on sale today. At full price the EG4 WallMount All Weather falls to about 3.19, the EG4 WallMount Indoor to 3.46 and the Rich Solar ALPHA 5 PRO to 2.28.
 A bare battery is cells, a battery management system and a case. It skips the inverter, the charger, the screen and the app that an all-in-one unit carries, and that is where the savings come from. Add an inverter, a charger, cables and a safe place to mount it, and its real cost per watt-hour goes up.
 The Renogy 12V 200Ah is a pre-order at the moment. The store lists it as shipping on November 7, so plan around that date.
 Expansion batteries are a third case. The Pecron EP3800-48V holds 3,840 Wh for $799, about 4.81 Wh per dollar, and the Anker SOLIX BP3800 holds 3,840 Wh for $1,799.99, about 2.13. Each one only works plugged into a station from its own maker, such as the Pecron E3600LFP or the Anker SOLIX F3800 Plus, so its number only counts if you own or buy that station.
 Where Small Capacity Costs You
 The smallest units almost always cost more for every watt-hour inside. The EcoFlow RIVER 3 Plus holds 286 Wh for $299, about $1.05 per watt-hour. The BLUETTI Elite 30 V2 holds 288 Wh for $289.99, about $1.01, and the EcoFlow RIVER 2 Max does better at 499 Wh for $329, about 66 cents.
 Step up to the BLUETTI Elite 400 and you pay about 36 cents per watt-hour at its regular price, about a third of what the smallest units charge for the same energy. The reason is fixed parts: every unit needs a battery management system, an inverter and a case, whatever its size.
 Trade-offs Beyond Capacity Per Dollar: Output, Portability and Warranty
 Output is part of the price. The Anker SOLIX F3800 Plus holds 3,840 Wh for $2,599.99, only about 1.48 Wh per dollar, because part of that price pays for a 6,000W inverter that delivers 120V and 240V from one unit.
 Portability separates the field. The units near 1,000 Wh, such as the BLUETTI Elite 100 mini, the ALLPOWERS P1800 and the BLUETTI AC180, are the easiest to carry, while 3,000 Wh units like the Pecron E3600LFP and the Jackery HomePower 3000 weigh much more and suit staying in one place. The bare batteries are built to be mounted, not moved.
 Warranty differs by maker. BLUETTI lists 5 years on the Elite 400, AC180 and Elite 200 V2 and 3 years on the Elite 100 mini, and Renogy lists 3 years, prorated, on the PowerStation 2000 and 5 years, prorated, on the 48V 50Ah Core and 12V 200Ah. EcoFlow lists 3 years on the DELTA 3 Max and DELTA 3 Ultra, or 5 if you register them in the EcoFlow app, and Jackery lists 3 years on the HomePower 3000, or 5 when bought at jackery.com.
 Check the store page for the warranty on the Pecron E3600LFP and the ALLPOWERS P1800 before you buy.
 Matching Capacity to What You Need to Run
 Capacity is the size of your fuel tank, and a cheap tank that is too small still leaves you stranded. Work out what you need to run first, then let price per watt-hour break the tie.
 About 300 Wh: phones, laptops, small lights, short outages.
 About 1,000 Wh: a CPAP overnight, a fridge for part of a day, small tools.
 2,000 Wh and up: a day of a fridge and the basics, longer outages.
 To get your own number, list every appliance that has to stay on, multiply its watts by the hours a day it runs, add them up, and add about a fifth more for inverter losses. Compare that total to the capacity column above.
 Match it to your load
 Capacity per dollar ranks hardware, not fit. Run your real list through the Paravolta Blueprint calculator to see which of these actually carries it, then compare the ones that do in the Paravolta shop .
 Questions people actually ask
 What does watt-hours per dollar actually measure?
 It is the battery size divided by the price: how much stored energy you get for each dollar. A higher number means more storage for the money. It says nothing about inverter size, weight or features.
 Why does the Pecron E3600LFP rank first?
 At 3,072 Wh for $999, it stores more energy per dollar than any other all-in-one unit on this list today. That is a sale price: at its full price of $1,999 it scores about 1.54, and the BLUETTI Elite 400 would lead at 2.74.
 Why do bare LiFePO4 batteries score higher than all-in-one units?
 They skip the inverter, screen, wheels and charger, so more of the price goes to cells. They are meant for a fixed setup with a separate inverter, which you have to buy and wire before they power anything.
 Should I just buy the highest Wh per dollar unit?
 Only if it covers your loads. A unit with a great ratio still will not carry a freezer through a long outage if it is too small for your daily use.
 Why does the full-price column move some units so much?
 Some units are on a deep sale. The Pecron E3600LFP is $999 today against $1,999 full price, and the ALLPOWERS P1800 is $439 against $1,059.98, so both scores fall by half or more when the sale ends. Check today’s price on the store page before you compare.
 Do the small units make sense for anyone?
 Yes, if your job is charging phones or running a CPAP for a night rather than powering a fridge. You pay more per watt-hour, but less in total, and they are easy to carry.

 Best Portable Power Stations of 2026, Lab-Tested and Reviewed
 We tested models from Anker, EcoFlow, and Goal Zero, among others, to find the ones that will provide power the longest and recharge quickly
 By 
 Allen St. John 
 Senior Home & Tech Writer 
 By 
 Yasmeen Khan 
 Home & Garden Writer

 Updated September 2, 2026 
 When you shop through retailer links on our site, we may earn affiliate commissions.

 A portable power station can quietly keep your devices running, but you have to pause every now and then to recharge the battery.
 Photo: EcoFlow
 If you’ve ever used a pocket-sized power bank to recharge your phone, you’ll appreciate the utility of a portable power station . It’s essentially a large rechargeable lithium-ion battery with an array of outlets you can use to power appliances and other devices in your home and on the road.
 It can keep your gear running at a campsite or a tailgate party and, yes, during a power outage, too (though only for a limited stretch of time). Keep in mind that portable power stations won’t keep electric appliances and devices running for nearly as long as comparably sized generators , says Paolo Fu, who leads generator and portable power station testing for Consumer Reports. But power stations can be a great alternative to generators during short outages, of say, a couple of hours, or may last longer if you’re powering only a few key essentials at once.
 “Portable power stations can be handy during an outage to charge your phone, make emergency calls, stay in touch with loved ones, and keep a fridge or freezer running a little longer,” Fu says. “They are best for outages that last for hours, not days.”
 In this article
 Best Portable Power Stations 
 What Can You Do With a Portable Power Station? 
 Portable Power Stations:
 Advantages 
 Disadvantages 
 Should You Buy a Portable Power Station? 
 How CR Tests Portable Power Stations 
 More on Generators & Emergency Power
 CR's Generator Ratings & Buying Guide 
 Best Portable Generators 
 Pros and Cons of Inverter Generators 
 Best Solar Panels 
 What to Eat During a Power Outage 
 Unlike a generator, a power station is sleek, quiet, and easy to use. It starts easily, without you having to worry about an engine that may have sat idle in the garage for months. It doesn’t saddle you with messy gasoline refills, clogged carburetors, or oil changes . Even more important, it eliminates the potentially deadly carbon monoxide fumes associated with generators.
 Before you rush out and buy one, though, consider the trade-offs. Power stations can be pricey and heavy, and the fastest way to recharge them is to plug them into an outlet, which is hard to do when the power’s out in your home. (You can slowly recharge them through their accompanying solar panels, and the solar panels can also extend the run time of your power station, but depending on the load, this may not be sufficient.)
 To help you weigh the pros and cons, we recently tested six popular models with their accompanying solar panels. They range in price from about $500 to more than $2,500. All have the capacity to provide backup power for key appliances in your home. They can also be quite large—ranging in size from a large car battery to a carry-on suitcase—and reasonably heavy, weighing 30 to nearly 100 pounds.
 For reviews of all the models we tested, check out our portable power station ratings and buying guide for more details.
 CR's Guide to Home Improvement
 Find  top-rated products and expert tips to help you save energy and money—and protect your home from extreme weather. 
 Best Portable Power Stations
 These are the best portable power stations from our tests, earning high marks for recharge speed, power delivery, power quality, portability, and ease of use. The prices (and our testing) include the power station plus its solar panels. The power stations can also be purchased separately, without the panels.
 What Can You Do With a Portable Power Station?
 The right-sized battery power station can deliver enough electricity to run essential systems and appliances, but only for a relatively short time. Smaller models can keep a laptop running and a few lights on, while much larger ones can be daisy-chained into a whole-house backup power solution.
 Your first task is to decide which devices and appliances you want to power and how much capacity you need to get the job done. Because a larger appliance like a refrigerator can kick on and off and cause a power surge, our experts recommend that you leave a little leeway between the total wattage of your appliances and the maximum power of your station. Energy Sage offers a guide on how much power appliances and other household electronics need.
 To help figure out what a portable power station can handle and for how long, take a look at the “claimed capacity” in watt hours (Wh) as well as the “claimed output” in watts in our ratings chart , Fu says. You’ll need to divide the power station’s capacity by its output to get a sense of how long the power station will run at full capacity.
 For example, the top model in our ratings, the EcoFlow Delta, has a claimed output of 3,600 watts and a claimed capacity of 3,600 watt-hours. If you want the EcoFlow working at full strength, delivering 3,600 watts to power all of the electronics you can—say, a refrigerator, laptop, television, five to 10 lights, and a medium window air conditioner—it would run for just one hour.
 If you want the EcoFlow to continuously power just your refrigerator, which draws about 700 watts, the power station would run for more than 5 hours on battery alone. (If you add the solar panel, it would extend the run time slightly, depending on solar conditions.) 
 A power station can also be used like an inverter generator to supply power at a campsite or a tailgate party. Indeed, power stations have become a staple on the road for those who revel in the adventures of van life . 
 They’re also a bit more flexible than generators at delivering power because they often supplement standard 120-volt, three-prong outlets with USB-A and USB-C ports for powering phones, laptops, and portable speakers.
 If you plan to take a portable power station on the road and use it outdoors, make sure you understand what kind of weather it can handle, Fu says. “Most solar panels we tested can handle any weather, but the power station itself may not be able to,” he says. “You don’t want to use the power station in the rain unless the manufacturer states that it’s waterproof.” 
 Or if you are using one in a dusty climate, make sure the manufacturer rates it for dust.
 Advantages of a Portable Power Station
 Here are the best reasons to invest in a portable power station:
 It’s quiet. Because it doesn’t have an engine, a portable power station is very quiet. Many don’t even have a cooling fan, so those—including the ones we’ve tested—are dead silent. (If your power station doesn’t have a cooling fan, Fu says to make sure to monitor it in the heat.) While tranquility may not be a huge consideration when your electricity is out, a near-silent power source at a campsite allows you to hear the lilting birdsong of a wood thrush instead of the rumble of a generator.
 It doesn’t emit dangerous carbon monoxide fumes. As a result, portable power stations don’t require the safety precautions of a generator, which include outdoor placement at least 20 feet from a home or garage, with the exhaust directed away from windows, doors, and air conditioners. You can run a power station in your kitchen, basement, or garage, so you don’t need an awning to keep the unit dry, as you would with a generator. That makes a power station a compelling alternative for apartment dwellers who want emergency backup power but lack the outdoor space to run a generator.
 It has excellent power quality. All of the power stations we’ve tested earn top marks for power quality, which is the ability to deliver clean power without the dips and spikes that can damage sensitive electronics. Their power quality is higher than most standard (noninverter) generators we’ve tested.
 Disadvantages of a Portable Power Station
 Here are the reasons you might choose to avoid a portable power station:
 It isn’t always convenient. The biggest disadvantage is that, like any battery, your power station will run out of power. And when that happens, you have to disconnect the unit and recharge it—a process that can take hours. That’s an inconvenience if you’re using the power station to charge your laptop, but it’s a major problem if you’re relying on it to keep food cold or power vital medical equipment. A generator has a big advantage here. Yes, it can run out of fuel, but when that happens, you just turn it off and refill the tank from a gas can, with only the briefest interruption of power.
 Its recharge rate can be slow. Not all portable power stations recharge at the same rate. When calculating Overall Scores, our testers assign the highest weight to recharge speed. Each of the models we’ve tested has portable solar panels that can recharge it, but the process is often slow, especially when the sky is overcast. You’re better off using the panels to extend the battery’s range, not to recharge it. And just as the power stations recharge at different rates, they deplete at different rates, too. Some are more efficient than others when powering the same load and can last longer.
 It’s heavy. And, for what it’s worth, portable power stations are not always easy to transport. Some heavier models come with wheels, like the 97-pound EcoFlow Delta Pro. But other models in our ratings don’t. CR evaluates handles as part of the portability rating because even lighter models—ranging from 30 to 60 pounds—should have one that’s easy to grip.
 It’s expensive. Finally, portable power stations are quite expensive. Our top-rated model—the EcoFlow Delta Pro—puts out 3,600 watts and costs more than $2,500. For comparison, you can buy a highly rated 3,900-watt inverter generator like the Generac iQ5200DF for about $1,000.
 Should You Buy a Portable Power Station?
 It ultimately comes down to how you plan to use it.
 Our ratings chart can help you zero in on a model that delivers high-quality power. But for many people, a gas-powered generator will be cheaper and more effective in a lengthy power outage, such as after a storm or other natural disaster.
 But if a portable power station’s most important virtues—quiet operation and the placement flexibility that comes with a lack of dangerous emissions—suit your needs, you might find it worthwhile to pay more than you would for a comparably sized generator.
 How CR Tests Portable Power Stations
 In our labs, CR test engineers evaluate five key measures to rate portable power stations: recharge speed, power delivery, power quality, portability, and ease of use. We don’t test the manufacturer’s run time claims, nor do we include noise evaluations in our ratings, because we found that, as a category, portable power stations run silently. 
 Recharge speed is based on how quickly the station charges while plugged into a 120-volt power source and while using the power station’s accompanying solar panels.
 Power delivery is based on how well the voltage is maintained and how well the unit handles surges in power. Higher power output means more equipment can be run simultaneously. Power quality reflects the station’s ability to deliver clean power over various loads. 
 To assess portability, we evaluate the power station’s ergonomics. To assess ease of use, we evaluate features including the number of outlets, USB port outputs, whether the power station has clear indicators of remaining power, and whether it comes with a companion app.
 Allen St. John
 Allen St. John has been a senior product editor at CR since 2016, focusing on digital privacy, audio devices, printers, and home products. He was a senior editor at Condé Nast and a contributing editor at publications including Road & Track and The Village Voice. A New York Times bestselling author, he's also written for The New York Times Magazine, The Wall Street Journal, and Rolling Stone. He lives in Montclair, N.J., with his wife, their two children, and their dog, Rugby.

 FAQ
 About HomePower 3000
 Does the HomePower 3000 support simultaneous AC input charging and AC output?
 It can. In Bypass Mode, HomePower 3000 allows simultaneous AC input charging and AC output to devices. However, during charging, the available output power may be slightly lower than its rated output​
 Is the HomePower 3000 fireproof? What is the fireproof level of the exterior material?
 The HomePower 3000 uses durable materials and has passed necessary certifications for safety, but it is not fully fireproof. Exposure to temperatures over 130°C (265°F) could cause risks such as fire or explosion​
 Is the HomePower 3000 expandable? Can I increase its capacity?
 No, the HomePower 3000 is a standalone system without the option to connect additional expansion batteries.
If you need expandable capacity, you can select our 2000 Plus or 5000 Plus series, which support battery expansion​
 Can the HomePower 3000 be used as UPS (Uninterruptible Power Supply)?
 Yes, HomePower 3000 supports UPS mode. When connected to AC input, it powers devices through grid electricity. In case of a sudden outage, it automatically switches to battery mode within 20ms. However, it does not support 0ms switching, and it’s not recommended for sensitive devices like data servers​
 Can the HomePower 3000 power an RV?
 The HomePower 3000 cannot directly charge an RV. To use it, you need to connect a grounding adapter. TT-30 RV port for 3600W Massive Output. (120V,30A)
 Can the HomePower 3000 power household circuits?
 Yes, the HomePower 3000 supplies power to home circuits by connecting to Manual Transfer Switch. Keep up to 6 essential circuits running during a blackout.
 Will low temperatures affect the performance of the HomePower 3000?
 Using the HomePower 3000 in low temperatures may affect charging and discharging performance. This is normal and does not affect usage. Simply move the device to a warmer environment to restore normal operation.
 Can I use this power station with medical devices, life-support equipment, business-critical systems, or other essential equipment?
 For safety reasons, Jackery portable power stations are not recommended for use with medical devices, life-support equipment, data servers, or other applications where a power interruption could result in personal injury, loss of life, or significant property damage.

 By Editorial Team · Updated October 21, 2026
 Affiliate disclosure: We independently research and test every product. When you buy through links on this page, we may earn a commission at no extra cost to you. Learn more .
 Quick answer
 The EcoFlow Delta 2 is the best portable power station for most people in 2026 — a 1,024Wh LiFePO4
battery with a real 1,800W AC output (2,700W with X-Boost) and a wall recharge to 80% in under an
hour, according to EcoFlow’s published specs. The Anker SOLIX C1000 matches it almost spec-for-spec
at a similar price with a longer warranty, and the EcoFlow River 3 Plus (286Wh) is the pick if you
just need a light, grab-and-go unit for phones and lights. Match capacity to your device wattage
first — most buyers are well served by 1,000Wh, and only fridge-plus-medical or multi-day off-grid use
needs 2,000Wh or more.
 Last updated 2026-10-10: corrected the Anker SOLIX C1000’s street price, which had been stuck at
a stale ~$699 — it now runs $399-479 per this site’s own dedicated C1000
review , undercutting the EcoFlow Delta 2 outright.
 A portable power station is a big rechargeable battery with real AC wall outlets, USB ports, and a
12V car socket built in — silent, fume-free backup power for camping, blackouts, CPAP machines, and
job sites. The market moved fast: the best 2026 units use LiFePO4 cells that last four to eight
times longer than the lithium in early models, and they recharge from a wall outlet in under an
hour instead of six. Below are the five we’d actually buy, tested against rated specs on usable
capacity, sustained output, and recharge time.
 Our top picks at a glance

 Anker SOLIX C1000 Best value 1,056Wh 1,800W (2,400W surge) LiFePO4 $399-479 ★★★★★

 Power stations by the numbers
 1,000Wh: the sweet-spot capacity for most buyers — enough to run a CPAP for a couple of nights, keep phones and a laptop alive through a multi-day outage, or power a mini fridge for a day.
 ~500-800 cycles vs 3,000-4,000 cycles: the lifespan gap between older NMC lithium and modern LiFePO4 cells before they drop to 80% capacity. It’s the single biggest reason to buy a current-generation unit.
 80%: the share of the rated wattage you should plan to actually use — inverter overhead and voltage sag mean a “1,800W” unit runs a ~1,500W load reliably, not a 1,790W one.
 ~50-80 minutes: how long the fastest 1kWh units (EcoFlow, Anker) now take to recharge from a wall outlet — a genuine step change from the 5-6 hours older stations needed.
 1. EcoFlow Delta 2 — Best Overall
 EcoFlow Delta 2 (1,024Wh)
 Best overall · ~$699 · 1,024Wh LiFePO4 · 1,800W AC
 1,800W of continuous AC output, and EcoFlow's X-Boost trick runs up to 2,700W of resistive-heating loads (kettles, hair dryers) that would trip a smaller inverter.
 Wall recharge to 80% in about 50 minutes — among the fastest of any 1kWh station.
 Expandable to 3,040Wh with add-on batteries, so it grows from a camping unit into home backup without replacing anything.
 The Delta 2 is our default pick because it nails every fundamental. The LiFePO4 pack is rated for
3,000 cycles to 80% — years of daily use — and the app gives you granular control over charge
limits and output. The standout is recharge speed: plug it into any wall outlet and it’s back to
80% by the time you’ve packed the car. It’s expandable, well-supported, and frequently discounted
below its $999 list price, which is why it wins over pricier competitors.
 2. Anker SOLIX C1000 — Best Value
 Anker SOLIX C1000 (1,056Wh)
 Best value · $799 list, $399-479 street · 1,056Wh LiFePO4 · 1,800W AC
 Full recharge in about 58 minutes flat — the fastest wall charge on this list.
 1,800W output with a 2,400W SurgePad mode for tools and appliances with a startup spike.
 Compact, dense, and well-built, with a 5-year warranty that beats most rivals.
 The C1000 lists at $799 but street pricing has run $399-479 through most of 2026 per this site’s own
 C1000 review — a real drop from its earlier ~$699 street price,
now undercutting the Delta 2 outright. It’s expandable to 2,112Wh with an add-on battery, and Anker’s
5-year warranty and reputation for support make it the safe pick if you want to buy once and forget
about it. The only reason it isn’t our outright winner is EcoFlow’s slightly larger accessory ecosystem
— for most buyers the C1000 is just as good, and now the cheaper one. If 1,056Wh is more capacity than you need, Anker’s own smaller
 SOLIX C800 lineup offers the same 5-year warranty at a lower
price point.
 3. Jackery Explorer 1000 v2 — Best for Beginners
 Jackery Explorer 1000 v2 (1,070Wh)
 Best for beginners · ~$799 · 1,070Wh LiFePO4 · 1,500W AC
 Genuinely the simplest to live with — clear display, foolproof ports, and Jackery's huge support presence.
 Upgraded to LiFePO4 in the v2, with a 3,000W surge that handles most startup spikes.
 Lightweight at ~23.8 lb and pairs cleanly with Jackery's SolarSaga panels for a plug-and-play solar generator.
 If this is your first power station, buy the Explorer 1000 v2. Jackery’s interface is the most
approachable in the category, the v2 finally moved to long-life LiFePO4, and the light weight makes
it the easiest to actually carry. Its 1,500W inverter is a touch smaller than the EcoFlow and Anker,
so very high-wattage appliances are off the table, but for phones, laptops, a CPAP, lights, and a mini
fridge it’s more than enough.
 4. Bluetti AC180 — Best Budget 1kWh
 Bluetti AC180 (1,152Wh)
 Best budget 1kWh · ~$499 · 1,152Wh LiFePO4 · 1,800W AC
 The most capacity-per-dollar here — 1,152Wh and a full 1,800W inverter for well under the others.
 Power Lifting mode pushes up to 2,700W of resistive loads.
 Frequently drops to ~$499 on sale, making it the best entry into a full 1kWh station.
 The AC180 undercuts everything else on this list while matching them on the specs that count. Recharge
is slower than the EcoFlow and Anker (roughly 1.5 hours from the wall), and Bluetti’s app is a step
behind, but you’re getting the most watt-hours for your money. If budget is the deciding factor and
you don’t need sub-hour charging, this is the value buy. See our
 best Bluetti power station guide for how the AC180 compares
against Bluetti’s other eight current models.
 5. EcoFlow River 3 Plus — Best Small / Grab-and-Go
 EcoFlow River 3 Plus (286Wh)
 Best compact · ~$269-299 · 286Wh LiFePO4 · 600W AC
 Tiny and light enough to toss in a backpack, yet runs a 600W load (1,200W surge) via X-Boost.
 LiFePO4 cells even at this size, so it survives years of camping trips.
 Expandable with a bolt-on battery to 572Wh if your needs grow.
 Not everyone needs a kilowatt-hour brick. The River 3 Plus is the one to grab for weekend camping,
charging phones and a drone, or running CPAP for a night or two. At ~286Wh it won’t run anything with
a heating element for long, but it’s small, cheap, and uses the same long-life LiFePO4 chemistry as
its big siblings. Read our full EcoFlow River 3 Plus review 
for the complete breakdown, or see the base EcoFlow River 3
review for an even lighter, cheaper option that drops to 245Wh and
300W for less money.
 How to choose a portable power station
 Capacity (watt-hours): how much energy it stores. Match it to your total load × hours. 1,000Wh covers most buyers — see our full sizing guide for a device-by-device wattage breakdown.
 Output (watts): how much it can run at once. A 1,800W inverter handles most household devices; check the surge rating for anything with a motor or heating element.
 Battery chemistry: buy LiFePO4 unless it’s a tiny grab-and-go unit — it lasts far longer and is safer. See how long a power station actually lasts for the real-world years behind that rated cycle count.
 Budget doesn’t have to mean NMC: several sub-$300 units still use real LiFePO4 — see our best budget portable power station picks for which ones actually hold up.
 Recharge speed & solar input: the newest units hit 80% from the wall in under an hour; check the max solar input if you’ll pair panels (see our solar generator picks ).
 Expandability: if you might want home backup later, buy into a line that takes add-on batteries so you don’t start over.
 Whichever unit you buy, a little care goes a long way — see our power station maintenance
guide for the storage charge level, temperature limits, and
charging habits that keep a LiFePO4 battery hitting its full 3,000+ cycle lifespan.
 If home backup — not camping — is the main job, see our dedicated best power station for home backup picks, which focus on larger expandable units. Shopping specifically for an RV instead? Our best RV power station guide covers shore-power recharging and rooftop-AC sizing that general-purpose picks don’t. Still weighing a battery unit against a traditional gas generator? Our power station vs. generator breakdown compares noise, runtime, and indoor safety head-to-head. Renting an apartment where a gas generator isn’t an option at all? Our best solar generator for apartment living picks cover the quiet, closet-friendly units built for that exact situation. Only need a unit for a single trip or event? Our power station rental vs. buying breakdown covers when renting actually beats a purchase.
 Still deciding between brands? Read our head-to-head breakdowns: Jackery vs EcoFlow ,
 Anker SOLIX vs Bluetti , EcoFlow vs Bluetti ,
 Jackery vs Bluetti , Goal Zero vs Jackery , and
 EcoFlow vs Anker SOLIX . Or read our in-depth EcoFlow Delta 2
review for a closer look at our top overall pick, or our full
EcoFlow lineup guide if you’re deciding between EcoFlow’s ten
current models specifically. Or read our in-depth Anker
SOLIX C1000 review for the longest-warranty runner-up — or our
 Anker SOLIX C1000 Gen 2 review for the newer, higher-output
model at a lower price if you don’t need the expansion battery, or our full Anker SOLIX lineup
guide for how all seven current Anker SOLIX models compare. Our
 full Jackery lineup guide covers all six current Jackery models
and the naming traps that trip up more Jackery buyers than any other brand here. If
you’ve outgrown a 1kWh unit entirely, our EcoFlow Delta Pro review 
covers the whole-home step-up option, or see our EcoFlow Delta Pro 3
review for EcoFlow’s newer, faster-charging flagship above it.
Considering a Renogy Phoenix 1000 you’ve seen discounted online?
Our Renogy Phoenix 1000 review weighs its high surge rating
against a much shorter warranty than every unit above. Need less than a full 1kWh unit but more than
a pocket camping station? Our Bluetti AC70 review covers the 768Wh
middle ground. Fly DJI drones? Our DJI Power 1000 review covers the
1kWh unit that fast-charges Mavic and Air batteries, and why DJI’s own US store doesn’t sell the V2.
 The bottom line
 The EcoFlow Delta 2 is the best portable power station for most people in 2026 — fast-charging,
expandable, and endlessly discounted. The Anker SOLIX C1000 is its equal on value with a longer
warranty, the Jackery Explorer 1000 v2 is the friendliest first buy, the Bluetti AC180 is the
budget champion, and the EcoFlow River 3 Plus is the one to keep in your bag. Spotted one of these
models at Costco instead of Amazon? See our power stations at Costco 
guide before assuming the listing will still be there next month. Shopping at Walmart instead? Our
 power stations at Walmart guide covers which brands have a confirmed
direct presence there and what to check before buying from a third-party listing. Home Depot actually
carries all five major brands — see our power stations at Home Depot 
guide for why that doesn’t mean Home Depot is always the cheaper option.
 Frequently Asked Questions
 What is the best portable power station overall? For most people the EcoFlow Delta 2 is the best all-rounder in 2026 — a 1,024Wh LiFePO4 battery, a genuine 1,800W AC output (2,700W with X-Boost), and one of the fastest wall recharges in its class. If value matters more, the Anker SOLIX C1000 is nearly identical on paper and now runs $399-479 street, undercutting the Delta 2, with a recharge under an hour.
 How many watt-hours do I actually need? Add up the watts of the devices you want to run and multiply by the hours you need them. A phone is ~10Wh a charge, a CPAP ~30-60Wh a night, a mini fridge ~600-800Wh a day. Most people are well served by a 1,000Wh unit; only fridge-plus-medical or multi-day off-grid use needs 2,000Wh or more.
 Is LiFePO4 worth it over a standard lithium battery? Yes, if you keep the unit more than a couple of years. LiFePO4 (LFP) cells last roughly 3,000-4,000 cycles to 80% capacity versus ~500-800 for older NMC lithium, and they tolerate heat and full discharges far better. Every unit on this list except the smallest uses LiFePO4.
